title: Mirabai's songs
hook: a woman who left a palace counts her treasure

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai's songs: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. Whose did you walk in as? Day nine hundred thirty-two.

A strange inventory for a princess. Mira grew up, the stories say, among jewels and silks, in a house with a treasury. She walked away from all of it. And one of the songs sung in her voice is about getting rich. Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo. I've found it, I've found the treasure, the jewel of Ram's name. A woman who left a royal house describes what she has now in the language of money. Today, our last day with Mira: her accounts.
screen: `JEWELS, SILKS, A TREASURY.` → `SHE WALKS AWAY.` → `I'VE FOUND THE TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Listen to it like a statement from the bank. Credit: a priceless thing, given to me by my true guru, out of kindness. Balance: the savings of lifetime after lifetime, found at last. Debit: everything else the world offered, gone. Then come the terms of the account, terms no bank has ever offered. Spend it, and it doesn't run down. Thieves can't touch it. Day by day it grows. And then the song leaves the bank for a river. The boat is truth, the boatman is the true guru, and I have crossed the ocean of becoming. The last line: Mira's lord is Giridhar, and she sings his praise with joy upon joy. Two things are worth noticing. First, the names. Mira's beloved is Krishna, the mountain-lifter. Here she sings of the jewel of Ram's name. Some readers hear Ram's name here as the name of God itself, and the very last line still calls her lord Giridhar. The song holds both names without strain. Second, the treasure is given, not earned. A guru hands it over in kindness. All her own effort in the song is the receiving and the singing. Look at Mira's three days together. A cup of poison she drank laughing. A husband she chose against the world's shame. And now the ledger of a woman who lost a palace and counts herself rich, because she owns the one thing that grows when it's spent.
screen: `READ IT LIKE A BANK STATEMENT.` · `SPENT, IT DOESN'T RUN DOWN.` · `THE BOAT IS TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING THAT GROWS WHEN SPENT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe, and make a quiet ledger. On one side, something you've lost or let go of: a plan, a place, an earlier version of yourself. Don't hurry past it. On the other side, ask: is there something I have that spending doesn't use up? A love, a kindness someone once gave you, a practice, a faith, a name you say. Hold that one. Notice that sitting with it doesn't make it any smaller. If you pray, you can thank the one who gave it to you. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai's songs. In this one, the jewel of the name: a treasure no thief can steal, which grows each day it's spent.
Your line: Mirabai's songs. Today, spend something that grows when it's spent, like attention, patience or a kind word, and see whether you run out. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

screen: `DAY 932 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CHAITANYA AND THE BENGAL KIRTAN.`

howItsDone: Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo is sung as a bhajan at home gatherings, in temples and on concert stages, and in school and community prayer meetings in India.

pairs: truth, with the guru at the oars

myth: Mira sings that the treasure runs down as she spends it
spending doesn't use it up, thieves can't steal it, and it grows day by day.
in the song, the treasure is a gift from a guru
the song names Ram, though its last line calls her lord Giridhar
the song sings of the jewel of Ram's name, and its last line still sings of Giridhar.

fork.setup: you've left a palace and its treasury behind. someone asks what you have now. what do you say?
options: nothing, and I've made my peace with it.
a treasure: the jewel of the name, and it grows when spent.
fork.reveal: payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo: I've found the treasure. in Mira's ledger the palace is the small loss and the name is the fortune.

original.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: a jewel. Ram ratan dhan is the treasure of the jewel of Ram's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song about being happy without money.
what it means: a full set of accounts, with a treasure that grows when spent, ending on a boat across the ocean of becoming.
what a scholar hears: the treasure is given by a satguru, a true teacher, and Ram's name and Giridhar sit together in one song.

sources.ref: Padavali of Mirabai, the song 'Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo'

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm lines paraphrased: vastu amolak di mere satguru; janam janam ki punji; kharach na khute, chor na loote, din din badhat savayo; sat ki naav khevatiya satguru, bhavsagar tar ayo; Mira ke prabhu Giridhar nagar.
The treatment of 'Ram' as the name of God in a Krishna devotee's song is interpretive. Tradition sometimes names Ravidas as Mira's guru; deliberately not stated.
howItsDone says the song is sung in school and community prayer meetings; confirm.
Editor pass: 'Ram's name stands for the name of God' reframed as what some readers hear (teach and myth reveal); howItsDone no longer calls the song 'familiar'.
Audit pass: paraphrase checked line by line against Payoji maine; no change.
